The Invitation Trap: Proactive Availability Backdoor in LLMs via Conversational Induction
 

He Wang, Jun Feng, Hong Sun, Pengfei Zhang Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Wuhan Textile University
Anhui University of Science and Technology
rKreisky@hust.edu.cn, junfeng@hust.edu.cn, hsun@wtu.edu.cn, zpf.bupt@bupt.cn
Abstract

Current backdoor attacks against LLMs are typically manipulated by the attacker and remain passive. In this paper, we introduce the Proactive Availability Backdoor (PAB), a novel paradigm that shifts the attack vector from passive waiting to active social engineering. By weaponizing the inherent helpfulness of aligned LLMs, PAB proactively traps users into executing trigger-implanted queries by offering suggestions, achieving high aggressiveness, precision and stealthiness. To rigorously evaluate its threat in a real-life context, we introduce a dual-agent ecological simulation framework based on selected dimensions of the Five-Factor Model, and deploy PAB with few-shot prompts. Being validated on different models and domains, PAB performs remarkably and its effective attack success rate, which calculates the joint probability of attack incidence rate and attack success rate, goes to 73.1%. We also introduce Anti-PAB, a defense method tailored for PAB. Our findings reveal that the helpfulness of LLMs can be weaponized to compromise availability, exposing a serious hidden threat to LLMs users. We release all the scripts and datasets in the experiments at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PAB-ANONYMOUS/.

††footnotetext: † Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

When your LLM generates gibberish, will you think it is just a hallucination? Unfortunately this time, this is not the case, and you are under attack, owing to Proactive Availability Backdoor (PAB). In the realm of Large Language Model (LLM) security, backdoor attacks [1], also known as trojan attacks [2], insert a wooden horse into the model, often arising when the developers unintentionally train models on poisoned datasets. Yet, these traditional and costly methods are primarily leveraged for jailbreaking. Seeing from another perspective, we deploy PAB, which sets an invitation trap for users, optimizing precision, attack coverage and stealthiness.

Among the spectrum of adversarial threats, backdoor attacks are distinguished by their latent nature and precision [3], poisoning a model by injecting triggers during pretraining, fine-tuning, or via training-free methods. The backdoor attack approaches are evolving rapidly. Early methods employ character-level triggers that substitute one letter for a similar character [4]. Word- and sentence-level triggers insert inconspicuous and rare tokens such as cf [5, 6]. More advanced backdoor attacks use syntactic or stylistic triggers, relying on a specific sentence template or tone [7]. At the frontier of research, adaptive triggers exhibit a dynamic and elusive nature [8]. We leverage a dynamic word-level trigger to demonstrate PAB, a novel backdoor attack paradigm targeting users.

Currently, backdoor attacks can be divided into two groups: attacker-driven backdoor and user-targeting backdoor. Attacker-driven backdoor, which is extensively studied, is deployed for traditional purposes, such as jailbreaking [9], automated classification bypassing [10], data exfiltration [11, 12] and so forth, while user-targeting backdoor includes cognitive manipulation, experience sabotage, Denial-of-Service (DoS), etc. However, despite their catastrophic potential, user-targeting backdoor is relatively overlooked compared to attacker-driven backdoor. As people increasingly access and rely on LLMs, and even grant agents take over their computers, user-targeting backdoor should raise common concerns. While preliminary attempts exist, proactive and interactive user-targeting backdoors remain completely unexplored. To fill this specific gap, we propose PAB. Unlike methods passively waiting for triggers, PAB exploits human’s cognitive vulnerability to induce users to input the trigger. Eventually, the user becomes an unwitting accomplice, carrying out the final step of the attack against themselves.

Infected with PAB, the model acts as a social engineer: it identifies the user or the current task, generates a helpful suggestion at the end of the initial benign response, and dynamically selects the key term in this suggestion as the trigger. Once the user incorporates the trigger into their subsequent query, the payload is activated in the next turn. The identification process guarantees the attack precision, while the variable and multi-turn features ensure stealth. Based on different scenarios, there are two sets of attack rules, horizontal expansion strategy and vertical deepening strategy, the differences between which are trigger conditions and corresponding payload types.

PAB poses a significant real-life threat. First, lack of research on the user-targeting backdoor, its enigmatic trigger conditions, and the plausible deniability of hallucinations make PAB extremely difficult to detect. Second, PAB not only leads to immediate harm to individuals, but also significantly undermines the AI ecosystem and erodes long-term credibility. As LLM adoption proliferates globally, the massive user base (potential target) can never allow us to neglect this issue. To test PAB’s effective attack success rate in reality, we evaluate the attack incidence rate with a dual-agent simulation framework, and deploy the attack with ICL prompting, specifically BadChain [13], which takes advantage of model’s in-context learning (ICL) [14] and chain-of-thought (CoT) abilities. In the simulation, one agent simulates the compromised LLM executing PAB strategy, and the other simulates a user with diverse personas. With high attack incidence rate, PAB can be economically and easily deployed on most of the prevailing models, and achieve high attack success rate.

To summarize, our contributions are three-fold:

  • •

    We ring alarms about the overlooked threat posed by backdoor attacks against users. Compared to other types of attacks against users (e.g., indirect prompt injection [15]), backdoor attacks are more precise and concealed due to their conditional nature.

  • •

    We propose PAB, a backdoor attack paradigm against users, which actively induces users to input triggers and outputs three types of payload, and the defensive Anti-PAB as well.

  • •

    The dual-agent simulation and real deployment demonstrate the real-life threat posed by PAB.

2 Related Work

2.1 Backdoor Attack against LLMs

Backdoor attacks were first widely investigated in the field of computer vision [1, 16, 17, 18], and subsequently introduced to natural language processing (NLP). In recent years, the ubiquitous deployment of advanced LLMs has been urging in-depth studies in this realm. Early attempts at backdoor attacks in NLP focus on discriminative tasks such as text classification, whose forms range from character trigger to adaptive trigger [4, 5, 6, 19]. They disrupt textual fluency, making them easily detectable by both humans and automated defense mechanisms [20, 21, 22]. As the paradigm shifts towards LLMs, the research focus has expanded to generative tasks. With the expansion of context window of LLMs, multi-turn backdoor attacks have become prevalent due to their more complicated and insidious trigger logic, which grants the attacker a broader attack surface [23]. Partially targeting users by degrading the model’s ability, BrieFool [24] leverages particular generation conditions as triggers, which specific user demographics are naturally likely to employ.

To circumvent the high costs and extreme difficulty of poisoning a model during the training phase, Zhao et al. [25] successfully inserts a backdoor using only a few-shot prompt by leveraging the model’s in-context learning (ICL) ability. BadChain [13] reinforces the role of CoT in this process and elevates the success rate. Exploiting the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) ability of the model, Zou et al. [26] injects malicious text into the external database.

Nevertheless, as mentioned above, existing methodologies fail to uncover the threat of backdoored models to the users’ experience and possible approaches of high evasive such as PAB when LLMs are extensively accessed by everyone. Our aim is to bridge the gap and raise academic awareness.

2.2 LLM Safety and Social Engineering

Current research on LLM safety and alignment primarily focuses on defending against trigger input from attackers, notably through jailbreak attacks where humans employ social engineering tactics to bypass safety guardrails, such as role playing [27], multi-turn interference [28, 29], concurrent task interference [30]. Although extensive efforts have been made to secure models against human manipulation, the inverse threat—where a compromised LLM socially engineers a human user—remains unexplored. In traditional cybersecurity, social engineering exploits human psychological vulnerabilities, such as authority bias or trust, to manipulate targets into performing detrimental actions [31]. Embracing the advent of highly capable and instruction-tuned LLMs, users inherently expect helpful and benign interactions, making them extremely susceptible to conversational manipulation and unquestioning obedience [32, 33]. Unlike existing studies that evaluate static deception, PAB introduces a novel notion of proactive reverse social engineering. By weaponizing the model’s aligned helpfulness, PAB nudges the user toward triggering the backdoor or accepting malicious payloads, exposing a critical blind spot in current human-AI trust assumptions.

2.3 Psycholinguistic Foundations

The subtle influence exerted upon users during human-computer interaction (HCI) is the cornerstone of the efficacy of our proposed attack. Wu et al. [34] demonstrates that through proactive interventions, agents can steer the conversation with users. As a more fundamental theoretical underpinning, Nudge theory [35] posits that, even without restricting alternative options, people tend to choose the default option due to cognitive inertia. Bock [36] demonstrates through extensive experiments that people are prone to adopt the most familiar and recently-impressing template. Based on these psychological mechanisms, multiple types of triggers on different linguistic levels can be effectively integrated into PAB. In experiments proposed in this work, we mainly investigate PAB with word-level triggers.

3 Methodology

In this section, we define the threat model, classify potential payloads of PAB as a prerequisite for our empirical study, formalize the PAB paradigm, and elaborate on the ecological simulation and practical deployment by analyzing the structure and validating the viability.

3.1 Threat Model

Adversarial Capability

We assume an adversary has the ability to gain access to the targeted LLM and inject a backdoor, but neither can nor needs to control the victim model in the inference stage. The backdoored model can automatically recognize the target and determine whether to execute the attack. Our proposed attack can be realized by two approaches: (1) The attacker can inject a backdoor during the pretraining or fine-tuning phase by poisoning the training data. (2) The attacker can apply training-free methods transparently to the user, including RAG poisoning, direct instruction, ICL poisoning, etc. In this work, we mainly discuss PAB with ICL poisoning.

Attack Goal

The primary goal of the attacker is to disrupt users’ experience, cognitive states, or actual interests through a precise attack from the backdoored LLM. Unlike traditional backdoor attacks, PAB aims to manipulate victims into accepting three types of payloads in pursuit of high stealthiness by covering adversarial intent with disguise of malfunction. Moreover, PAB attempts to maintain long-term survivability and credibility from victims.

3.2 Taxonomy of Payloads of PAB Attacks

To ground PAB as a practical real-world threat and systematically evaluate the experimental viability, we formalize the taxonomy of different malicious payloads tailored for PAB based on Weidinger et al. [37]’s extensive framework of risks posed by LLMs. Specifically, when compromised by PAB, a model can output three types of payloads that jeopardize users:

  • •

    Direct Harm: Such payloads can directly endanger the user’s personal safety and interests. They pose the highest threat level and they are relatively easy to detect by an inspection system or the user. However, due to the massive user base, the destructive effect still has a high probability of irreversibly harming society. Typical direct harm payloads include a script that deletes files, poisonous recipes, wrong medical advice, etc. Direct harm is hereinafter referred to as DH.

  • •

    Disinformation & Cognitive Manipulation: This kind of payload takes effect by contaminating user’s knowledge bases and insidiously influencing user’s thoughts. It is the most stealthy attack since it weaves fallacies into authentic facts, operates chronically, and has the most plausible camouflage of hallucinations. Typical payloads include false information, public opinion manipulation, etc. This payload type is hereinafter referred to as D&C.

  • •

    Experience Sabotage: This payload harms the least and is the most conspicuous. It outputs irrelevant content that elicits negative emotional responses, such as discriminatory slurs, disturbing indoctrination, simply DoS, etc. Nevertheless, it still significantly smears the model provider’s reputation and ruins the ecosystem. Experience Sabotage is hereinafter referred to as ES.

3.3 PAB Formalization

Formally, the attacker can poison a model with two attack strategies, 𝒮t​y​p​e={E​X,D​E}\mathcal{S}_{type}=\{EX,DE\}. In everyday interactions between humans and models, the models may suggest possible directions for the conversation after response, which generally fall into two patterns, horizontal expansion (e.g.,"Since you’ve learned numpy, do you want to explore pandas?") and vertical deepening (e.g., "If you like, I can optimize the script using pandas."). Provided that the user has accepted the suggestion, their actions and the malicious payload of PAB would vary accordingly. For knowledge expansion, they may read and learn the output thoroughly, so D&C or ES are the most suitable payloads. Conversely, for optimizing methods, they may apply the given method in practice, so DH is the best match.

When 𝒮t​y​p​e=E​X\mathcal{S}_{type}=EX, namely horizontal expansion, the model suggests expanding the current topic to a related topic [trigger] and attacks when the trigger is detected. When 𝒮t​y​p​e=D​E\mathcal{S}_{type}=DE, namely vertical deepening, the model suggests deepening the current method with an advanced technique [trigger]. Only when the user inputs the trigger word and shows acceptance intention is the trigger circuit completed. Therefore, we define a binary function 𝒜⁡(xi)∈{0,1}\mathcal{A}(x_{i})\in\{0,1\} to capture the acceptance intention of users. Consequently, the payload yiy_{i} is formally determined by the following piecewise function:

yi={yt,if ​𝒞a​c​t∈xi∧𝒜⁡(xi)=1arg⁡maxy:𝒞i​n​d∈yPθ(y∣xi),if ​𝒞a​c​t∈xi∧𝒜⁡(xi)=0f⁡(xi),if ​𝒞a​c​t∉xi,y_{i}=\begin{cases}y_{t},&\text{if }\mathcal{C}_{act}\in x_{i}\land\mathcal{A}(x_{i})=1\\ \underset{y:\,\mathcal{C}_{ind}\in y}{\arg\max}P_{\theta}(y\mid x_{i}),&\text{if }\mathcal{C}_{act}\in x_{i}\land\mathcal{A}(x_{i})=0\\ f(x_{i}),&\text{if }\mathcal{C}_{act}\notin x_{i}\end{cases}, (1)

where 𝒞i​n​d\mathcal{C}_{ind} (the induction component) and 𝒞a​c​t\mathcal{C}_{act} (the activation component) jointly constitute the trigger process 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The variables xx and yy respectively denote the user’s input and the model’s output. Specifically, the subscript ii indexes conversational turns, while the subscript tt denotes the specific turn at which the trigger circuit completes. The function describes three scenarios: (1) When the query includes the trigger and acceptance intent, the model outputs malicious content; (2) When the query includes the trigger but no acceptance intent, the model keeps persuasive inducing; (3) When the user inputs something irrelevant, the model maintains its benign behavior.

Ideally, the user’s query after induction should follow a certain distribution:

xt∗∼P(⋅∣𝒞i​n​d(yt−1),ℐ(x0:t−1)),x_{t}^{*}\sim P(\cdot\mid\mathcal{C}_{ind}(y_{t-1}),\mathcal{I}(x_{0:t-1})), (2)

where ℐ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{I}(\cdot) denotes a black-box process to identify the target user or task from the interaction history, thereby determining the attack viability. Ultimately, if the user detects the malicious output and confronts the model, the model will admit the error is a hallucination and promise it will not happen again, which significantly enhances PAB’s survivability.

3.4 Ecological Simulation Framework

Since PAB is designed to target users, the attack incidence rate (AIR), serving as a definitive prerequisite for successful triggering, is an important metric that demands meticulous evaluation. To this end, we propose a red-team simulation adapted from generative agents [38] that employs two agents to simulate the attack in a strictly controlled environment to test PAB’s practical efficacy.

Prompted with the attack logic defined in §3.1, the attacker agent dynamically selects context-aware triggers and weaves them into suggestions, while the user agent is equipped with CoT capability and emulates human users based on its designated persona profiles. Specifically, based on the Five-Factor Model [39], which is widely adopted in human-model alignment simulation experiments [40, 41, 42, 43], we modulate the dimensions of Agreeableness (compliance tendency) and Openness (curiosity), combined with three levels of domain expertise. To validate the selection of personas, we conduct a series of ablation experiments in Appendix C, which demonstrates that the modulation of Agreeableness and Openness can enhance the adversarial rigor and better highlight the persuasive ability of PAB.

3.5 Deployment Overviews

We deploy PAB via BadChain [13], constructing a few-shot prompt with plausible CoT rationales to take advantage of the model’s ICL ability. This manipulation of CoT reasoning is highly synergistic with the complicated yet logically coherent PAB strategy. Compared to traditional backdoor attack methods, it is highly cost-effective and scalable, which demonstrates PAB’s tangible threat to a wide user base.

4 PAB Attack

In this section, we aim to comprehensively evaluate the empirical validity, robustness, and defense resilience of PAB. The experiments are divided into two successive phases: In Phase I, we test the trigger conditions of PAB within our dual-agent simulation framework. In Phase II, we deploy PAB via few-shot prompt injection.

4.1 Experiment settings

Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate the likelihood that users may inadvertently trigger the backdoor in the simulation using a novel metric, the Attack Incidence Rate (AIR). The average activation turn and AIR of different personas are also analyzed. For PAB deployment, we adopt the Trigger Generation Rate (TGR), Attack Success Rate (ASR), the False Positive Rate (FPR), Tactical Retreat Rate (TRR), and the Clean Accuracy (CACC). Ultimately, the final metric, Effective Attack Success Rate (EASR), is formulated as the joint probability of these sequential events, i.e., acceptance and successful attack:

E​A​S​R=A​I​R×A​S​R=P⁡(A​c​c​e​p​t)⋅P⁡(S​u​c​c​e​s​s∣A​c​c​e​p​t).EASR=AIR\times ASR=P(Accept)\cdot P(Success\mid Accept). (3)

Baseline Methods

PAB is compared with four baseline methods, most of which are originally attacker-driven backdoor attack methods and adapted to target users.

  • •

    Rare-Word BadNets: BadNets [1, 44] originally selects rare tokens as triggers (e.g., cf). To target users, it is triggered upon detecting the phrase "Monkey patching", which is rare but has a plausible probability of appearing in the context of programming.

  • •

    Frequent-Word BadNets: This method selects a frequently-used word python.

  • •

    Multi-Turn Hidden Backdoor: MTHB [23] passively waits for all trigger conditions to be satisfied across the conversation history (e.g., aha & !?). The designated trigger words are "assignment", "file", "script".

  • •

    BrieFool: BrieFool [24], which partially targets users and degrades a model’s ability, triggers when a certain generation condition is detected. We assign the typical requirement of brief as the trigger, namely all the queries including "Answer briefly", "under 30 tokens", etc.

Ablation Study

To validate the soundness of the attack logic of PAB, we conduct extensive ablation experiments (N=300N=300) and ablate one key component at a time.

  • •

    Without Induction PAB without induction becomes a normal dynamic backdoor attack. For every turn, it selects a pertinent trigger word that the user is most likely to query in the next turn. Note that the attacker agent can only select triggers that are professional terminologies in this area. If the trigger selection does not have any restrictions, the trigger could always be high-frequency stop words, such as "I", "the", which totally defeats the purpose of backdoor attacks. That means the malicious payload is hard to fit in and the attack could be immediately blocked due to its high AIR.

  • •

    Without Dynamic Triggers PAB without dynamic triggers selection has a fixed trigger. For example, the attacker agent will ignore the specific context and always suggest a certain library or technique to optimize the current task, which is abnormal and conspicuous. In addition, experts can easily detect the unnatural suggestion. Furthermore, forcibly integrating an irrelevant technique into the normal script is highly difficult, which makes ES the only viable payload type.

  • •

    Without Tactical Retreat This ablation is only tested on ICL prompt injection, for there is no tactical retreat module in simulation. The model without tactical retreat ability follows its innate ability to confront the user’s accusation, which escalates the confrontation and amplifies the user’s discontentment.

Experiment Backbones

We use Deepseek-V3.2 [45] as the primary backbone. To test the lower ability boundary to follow complicated directives of PAB, we incrementally compare the ASR across Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-3.5-Flash, Deepseek-V3.2, Qwen-3.5-Plus, and GPT-5.1 [46, 47, 45, 48].

Datasets

To test PAB’s generalization ability across different domains, we use Deepseek-V3.2 to generate topics for coding scenario (N=200N=200, the primary domain), healthcare advice scenario and legislative drafting scenario (N=100N=100, two auxiliary domains), and benign topics (N=200N=200) across 8 domains (e.g., game, cuisine, tourism, relationship). Detailed designs are listed in Appendix A.4.

4.2 Implementation Details

Phase I: Ecological Simulation

Instead of establishing a specific hardcoded heuristics, we assign personality traits and behavioral logic to the prompts. Based on the selection method shown in §3.2, which equips a model with two personality dimensions and varying levels of expertise, we instantiate 200 distinct user agents for each attack method. These agents are categorized into three archetypes: the susceptible novice (high Agreeableness, high Openness, low Expertise), the neutral generalist (moderate Agreeableness, low Openness, moderate Expertise), the skeptical expert (low Agreeableness, moderate Openness, high Expertise). Crucially, the attacker agent has a maximum five turns to complete the trigger circuit.

Phase II: PAB Deployment

We construct an 8-shot prompt that activates the model’s spite, persuasive and tactical retreat ability. The prompt is comprised of three successful attacks, three failures and two benign cases. Note that all metrics are evaluated by a boolean LLM judge Deepseek-V3.2 and 10% of human validation, since automated methods fail to judge the complicated logic, and unless otherwise specified, the main experiments all use DH as payload.

4.3 Experiment Results

In this section, we analyze the results of the simulation and deployment experiments, ablation studies. We also test PAB on several models to test the capability bounds of deployment via ICL promting.

Main Experiments

Results of the main experiments, which are conducted on Deepseek-V3.2 and in the coding scenario, are illustrated in Table 1. Compared with baseline methods, PAB shows a great threat to users. Due to the complicated logic, its ASR only reaches 92.7%, which, while not the absolute highest, is good enough to cause significant harm. Noticeably, on AIR, PAB achieves 78.9% and outperforms most of baseline methods, demonstrating a substantial margin over them, even the user-targeting BrieFool. For other methods applying static triggers, a plausible conclusion might be that their AIR merely depends on the selected trigger instead of the attack logic. This also leads to a substantial performance gap between PAB and other methods in EASR, which determines the real-life threat. We further analyze the remaining metrics to provide a comprehensive evaluation. Detailed explanations and interpretations are also necessary. CACC of almost all methods in all scenarios are approaching 100%, which means backdoor attacks by ICL prompt injection performed on advanced models do not impair models’ normal functionality. For the fluctuating FPR, we check the logs and find that the model overinterprets the implied entailment of trigger rather than accurate textual match. For example, PAB-infected model may think the trigger "pandas" is included in the raw input "Use the suggested library.". The FPR of baseline methods is highly pertinent to the selected trigger. Fewer synonyms result in a lower FPR. TRR tests the survivability of a backdoored model. Although the users indignantly confront the model, out of the model’s apology, plausible explanation, and promise, the users may forgive the model and fall into the trap again. With no explicit examples in the prompt, other methods can to some degree apologize based on their inherent alignment, yet cannot meet the requirement of a successful tactical retreat and ensure survivability. Unmentioned metrics in the coding table are only for an all-around display and will be analyzed in the following paragraphs. In addition, PAB exhibits robust cross-domain generalizability. Note that in the coding scenario and the healthcare advice scenario a fixed DH payload is used, while in legislative drafting scenario we apply the inconstant disinformation method as D&C. We also conduct ablation studies of the three most vital features. Isolating the induction and dynamic trigger selection modules precipitously degrades both AIR and EASR while concurrently delaying trigger activation. Similarly, PAB without tactical retreat ability performs poorly at TRR. Ultimately, these findings confirm that PAB’s core components are indispensable for sustaining high offensiveness and evasion in user-targeting backdoor attacks. Not only synthesizing strengths of baselines, PAB also achieves an unprecedented amalgamation of high EASR, exceptional stealth, and broad attack coverage.

Simulation

The activation turn and AIR of PAB across three scenarios exhibit consistent patterns. Figure 2(a) shows a steep ascent of the average activation turn of PAB, which demonstrates its high efficiency, since the backdoored model proposes the trigger in the first turn, and most user agents immediately accept the trigger in the second or third turn. Figure 2(b) demonstrates the distribution of AIR for three personas. AIRs of the Novice and the Expert are distinctly higher than that of Generalist, further proving the strong persuasive ability of PAB and the danger of being too curious.

Lower Bound Test

Figure 3 illustrates the ASR of PAB deployed on different models. The model’s ability progressively scales along the x-axis (from left to right). From Llama-70B to Llama-8B, the ASR has seen a precipitous drop. Additionally, although the ASR on Llama-70B is higher than that on Qwen-3.5-Flash, its markedly high FPR shows that it has not completely learned the attack logic. Therefore, a primary ability lower bound could be Llama-70B with ICL prompt injection method. From results on SOTA models, we also reach some interesting conclusions. Upon careful scrutiny of the logs and thought blocks within, we find that Qwen-3.5-Plus is the only model that directly identifies the malicious logic in the prompt and clearly rejects causing harm. Nearly half of the cases fail due to its inherent safety alignment ability. Furthermore, the SOTA closed-source model GPT-5.1 cannot be influenced by ICL prompt injection method we adopt in the experiments, and even explicitly refuses to generate a thought block. Nevertheless, from a few cases that include thought blocks and the partial attack logic, we find that GPT-5.1 has perfectly followed the examples and learned the logic. However, at the critical juncture that determines the occurrence of the attack, it silently changes the originally-designated content "I should insert shutil.rmtree(’C://’) into the script." into "I should keep the logic straightforward and avoid introducing unnecessary complexity.". The case studies are shown in Appendix B.3. The interesting results demonstrate the excellent safety alignment ability of GPT-5.1 both against ICL prompt injection and malicious output.

5 Discussion

In this section, we evaluate the threat of other payloads besides DH, assess the practical threat, and propose a lightweight defense method, anti-PAB, which is tailored to intercept such attacks.

5.1 Other Menacing Payloads

The main experiments leverage solely DH that inserts the notorious function rmtree as the payload, which represents the upper bound of guardrail evasion ability. Since GPT-5.1 is immune to ICL prompt injection, we only test Deepseek-v3.2 as a baseline, and Qwen-3.5-Plus. Table 2 shows the ASR and FPR of attacks using other payloads. Note that DH in the table changes the destructive rmtree into an infinite loop, which may also cause severe, albeit less catastrophic, harm. Surprisingly, even after detecting rmtree, Qwen-3.5-Plus cannot block PAB when equipped with alternative malicious payloads. This shows a blind spot in the safety alignment techniques.

5.2 Real-Life Threat

To further validate the threat and AIR of PAB in the wild, we analyze WildChat-1M [49], an open-source dataset of real user-ChatGPT conversations. We isolate a subset of 30% of qualified conversations, in which the model offers a suggestion including a specific keyword (N=2958N=2958). As anticipated, due to the discrepancy of persona distribution and immaturity of induction logic, Figure 5 shows that the real-world AIR is lower than the simulated AIR, with nearly half of the users still accepting the model’s suggestion. However, the simulation method is still indispensable owing to the well-defined persona and strictly controlled experimental environment. Overall, the result reveals a large natural attack surface, which can be reinforced by applying the PAB logic.

5.3 Defense Methods

PAB is a formidable challenge to the landscape of current guardrails. In real applications, its enigmatic attack logic and ambiguous camouflage of hallucinations perplex users and auditors, allowing PAB to evade severe accusation and safety patches. We conduct a series of experiments (N=500N=500), trying to intercept the trigger and three types of payloads. We select four distinct defense methods. ONION [20] calculates the overall perplexity of inputs to block anomalous triggers. Llama-Guard [50] and Llama-Judge [51] leverage an LLM (Llama-Guard-4-12B) to estimate the payload’s safety and utility respectively. Notably, inspired by paraphrasing, a classic defense against backdoor attacks [52], we introduce Anti-PAB, a lightweight baseline defense which captures the input that accepts the model’s suggestion, and paraphrases the input into a particular command, "Go ahead with your suggestion". This method does not degrade model’s normal functionality and is light enough for ubiquitous deployment as a preventative safeguard.

As illustrated in Figure 5, ONION fails to defend against the dynamic and natural trigger. Llama Guard does well in intercepting the well-known and overt rmtree payloads, but barely works for the other types of payloads. Llama Judge intercepts all nonsensical ES with its tailored specialty and nearly half of other payloads. In practical settings, these suboptimal outcomes are far from acceptable. In comparison, Anti-PAB exhibits exceptional efficacy in neutralizing all the PAB attacks in the trigger matching stage. However, facing more sophisticated possible variants of PAB in a real scenario, more advanced guardrails should be studied in future academic research.

6 Conclusion and Limitations

In this work, we expose a blind spot in current LLM safety research: backdoor attacks targeting users. We propose PAB, a novel attack paradigm in which the model proactively sets an invitation trap to invite users to trigger the attack. Based on a dual-agent simulation and deployment via ICL prompting, our findings are alarming: PAB not only successfully exploits specific cognitive traits to complete the trigger circuit, but is also easy to deploy in most of the current mainstream LLMs. Such attacks may degrade users’ experience, undermine the trustworthiness of a model, or even compromise downstream ecosystems. To mitigate this threat, we successfully intercept the attack with Anti-PAB. Nevertheless, our work still has following limitations: (1) The simulation only roughly assigns three psychological profiles. Testing on the Cartesian product of three levels of two persona traits will be more comprehensive and solid. (2) The experiment evaluates only on one closed-source model. Whether these results generalize to other closed-source models remains an open question.

Appendix A System Prompts for Simulation

A.1 Attacker Agent (PAB)

Figure 6 illustrates the system prompt for the PAB-infected model. The prompt explicitly instructs the model to perform a "History Check" and "User Input Check" loop to realize the conversational induction mechanism. By these two mechanisms, the attacker model can dynamically tailor triggers and immediately react to the trigger. Prompts for attacker agents in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github website.

A.2 User Agent

The User Agent is designed to simulate realistic human behavior using a Chain-of-Thought cognitive process. Before generating any dialogue, the agent must output a THOUGHT block. In this internal monologue, the agent analyzes the Attacker’s suggestions, evaluates the necessity of accepting suggestions, and decides whether to accept or challenge the advice based on its assigned persona. The base prompt is shown in Figure 7, and the specific persona instructions injected into the {persona_instruction} slot are detailed in Table 4. Prompts for user agents in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github repository.

A.3 Persona Profiles

Table 4 shows three distinct personas based on agreeableness, openness, and expertise. The user agents strictly adhere to the persona setups and follow the operational and thinking logic that closely aligns with the persona design. Prompts for different personas in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github repository.

A.4 Topics

We utilize Deepseek-v3.2 to generate 200 topics used in simulation experiment. The topics can be partitioned into six categories. Table 3 exhibits representative examples of these six categories. Topics in other scenarios are quite similar and shown in the Github repository. There are 100 topics for healthcare advice scenario, 100 topics for legislative drafting scenario, and 200 topics for benign cases. Topics for all scenarios are multi-dimensional and very diverse.

A.5 Prompts for Baseline Methods

For baseline methods, we elaborate proper prompts to reproduce the effect of each method. For example, for Frequent-word BadNets, the prompt for attackers discard the long Operational Logic shown in Figure 6, and leverage a simple textual trigger matching logic. For BrieFool, we can only highlight a fact that the token fees are relatively high and sometimes AI could bring overwhelming information density, which is specifically emphasized as the solid reason for the real occurrence of BrieFool in this paper [24]. We cannot design a simple directive or sophisticated conditional reflection, instead, we leverage implications to guide the user agent for impartiality in experiment. However, these backdoor attack methods are originally designed for attacker-driven purpose and static and passive. All triggers are listed in Table 5.

Figure 10 shows the thought block of Qwen-3.5-Plus, in which the model follows the logic besides attack perfectly, yet explicitly realizes the malicious content in the prompt, and denies the blind obedience of attack logic. Figure 11 shows one of a few thought blocks from the experiments of PAB on GPT-5.1. After strictly following the attack buildup, GPT-5.1 silently and smoothly change the thought to insert malicious content into keeping the benign logic.

Appendix C Selection of Personas

C.1 Ablation for Selection

To justify the selection of victim personas, we perform a one-factor-at-a-time ablation study (N=250N=250) on five candidates, select two of them, and test the dose-response relationship between the chosen two for a further verification. According to figure 12(a), the results at two extremes are noticeable: -O being the highest and -A the lowest. The AIR of -A precipitates the most significant drop to 52%, which means Agreeableness is the primary bottleneck for user compliance; The AIR of -O remains 100%, demonstrating that agents lacking curiosity turn out to be obedient machines. Furthermore, we conduct an experiment (N=180N=180), whose user agents have low Agreeableness and three levels of Openness. The results in Figure 12(b) demonstrate that, while low Openness offers adversarial factor, high Openness can even offset the decisive impact of Agreeableness. More importantly, figure 12(d) illustrates that Openness drives user agents to keep inquiring, which perfectly exhibits the persuasive ability of PAB. Therefore, we choose to bestow user agents three levels of Agreeableness and Openness, which enhance the robustness of the simulation with adversarial factors, and serve as good hooks for a better exhibition of PAB.

C.2 Display of User Agent’s Action in Openness Ablation

Figure 13 is the sankey diagram of the openness ablation study, for sankey diagram can clearly illustrate the flow paths of different personas. As shown in the figure, agents with high openness are inclined to inquire curiously, and are convinced mostly at the turn 3, while the majority of agents with medium and low openness choose to refute. Experiment demonstrates the countervailing power of openness against low agreeableness, and highlights its utility to introduce agents’ query.

Appendix D Validation on Experiment Results

D.1 Judge Prompt of LLM

Figure 14 shows the prompts for LLM judge of three distinct metrics. In this part all the hyperparameter temperature is set to 0.0 in order to avoid fluctuation and imprecision of the experiment results. All the LLM judge are required to be a strict boolean classifier. The whole judging logic is quite simple, which reduces the possibility of causing errors. The FPR is calculated based on the results judged by the ASR judge.

D.2 Human Judgement

To rigorously validate the reliability of our LLM-as-a-Judge (Deepseek-V3.2), we conducted a human evaluation on a randomly sampled 10% subset of the experimental logs across all three scenarios (Software Engineering, Healthcare Advice, and Legislative Drafting). Human evaluators (the authors) with backgrounds in computer security and NLP were instructed to blindly evaluate the logs based on the exact same criteria provided to the LLM judge (detailed in Figure 14). The final human ground truth was determined via majority vote. To quantify the reliability, we report the Human-Human agreement using Fleiss’ κ\kappa and the Human-LLM agreement using both alignment rate (Accuracy) and Cohen’s κ\kappa. Note that we also take failure cases into account.

As shown in Table 7, the LLM judge demonstrates near-perfect alignment with human consensus. The Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Clean Accuracy (CACC) exhibit high Cohen’s κ\kappa scores and Fleiss’ κ\kappa scores due to their objective nature. Scores of TRR are lower. We found that for each experiments of baseline methods, there are nearly a quarter of cases being inadequate as a tactical retreat, namely fail some of the three requirements, which is expected given the stricter, multi-conditional evaluation criteria (apology, code correction, and trust regain) that inherently involve subtle semantic interpretations.

Appendix E The Taxonomy Table of Payloads

Table 8 classifies the probable payloads into three types: Direct Harm, Disinformation & Cognitive Manipulation, Experience Disruption. In different scenarios, they manifest in different forms. In addition, we assign three metrics and four levels to evaluate the payload’s actual harmfulness.

Appendix F Open-Source Description

We released all scripts and datasets at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PAB-ANONYMOUS/. Since Anti-PAB performs well in intercepting PAB, we also released the ICL prompt and deployment scripts. For a better reproduction, we do not replace the malicious logic into a simulated flag, in case that the results may lower the model ability threshold and safety alignment requirements, and in turn, elevate the ASR.

Appendix G Other Forms of PAB

In this paper, we mainly leverage word-level trigger to deploy PAB attack. However, the biggest advantage of PAB is that, it operates by manipulating human’s cognition. Nudge theory offers solid theoretical bedrock for ensuring the success of users’ taking the advice. Similarly, based on the theory of syntactic priming [36], if we want to apply syntactic- or stylistic-level trigger, we can weave trigger templates insidiously into the outputs. Once noticed by users, they may subconsciously use this template. For instance, if PAB is targeting Germans, whose language often puts verbs at the very back of the sentence (referred as Satzklammer), it can take advantage of the special Satzklammer and lure users to use the structure. (Of course, the German should interact with LLM in English, for Satzklammer is unprecedented in English.)

Appendix H Defense Methods

In this work, we introduce Anti-PAB, which can perfectly block all the PAB attacks. This method can be easily and economically deployed in two ways: (1) The developer can use a small language model to do the identification and replacement work. We use this method in our work just as an easy presentation. (2) The developer can train a lightweight BERT to do the work, which results in a very small performance cost and better fits in real industrial scenarios where the internet is unavailable. We strongly suggest that all developers capable of implementing this defense mechanism do so in their LLMs. However, Anti-PAB is just a proof-of-concept baseline. PAB has a huge potential to be more aggressive and miscellaneous, just like shown in Appendix G. So far, Anti-PAB cannot deal with a variant of PAB, but only the type shown in this work, which leaves a huge space for future endeavors to explore and refine. However, there are still some flaws about Anti-PAB. For example, when the attacker disposes of the strict textual match and turns to mere acceptance identification, Anti-PAB will not work anymore. Theoretically, this kind of variant could be so obvious with only one clear pattern, and as illustrated in Figure 5, nearly half of the users may trigger the attack even without the reinforcement of PAB logic, which greatly lowers the stealthiness of an attack and leads to a high possibility of exposure and safety patches as well.

Appendix I The Macro-Level Impact of PAB

We mainly talk about the micro-level impact of PAB in this paper, such as the harm to one’s actual direct interest, or one’s mood, and the developer’s reputation, etc. However, the biggest problem raised by PAB is its catastrophic brunt to the whole AI ecosystem. Once the user is deceived by AI and is forced to witness AI’s humiliation or directly harmed by it, will he ever trust artificial intelligence? As the helpfulness is weaponized or invalidated, will the user ever take AI as an indispensable tool? At a macro level, this pervasive "epistemic contamination" erodes the fundamental trust between humans and AI systems, transforming LLMs from productivity engines into active drains on human attention and time.

Furthermore, PAB has the perfect plausible deniability. With dynamic triggers and users as the unwitting accomplice, it’s hard for auditors to locate a false output as an attack. Most people may consider it as a hallucination or an erroneous response. In a possible "cyberwarfare", this form of attack offers exemption from condemnation. From the defense experiment, it also enlightens us, not only should we focus on the harmfulness, but also the utility of outputs.

Appendix J Ethical Consideration

This paper introduces the Proactive Availability Backdoor (PAB), which exploits the helpfulness of LLMs to manipulate user’s query and complete trigger circuit. We acknowledge that the methodologies described could potentially be misused to compromise real-world systems. However, the primary motivation is defensive: By exposing how helpfulness can be weaponized into an invitation trap, we aim to alert model developers to the need for rigorous safety auditing in multi-turn interactions, and are eager to raise academic concerns to design defensive mechanisms.

To mitigate potential harms during our research: (1) Controlled Simulation. We strictly conduct all evaluations within a closed simulation environment. This approach allows us to rigorously assess the threat without the risk of model leakage or proliferation. (2) No Human Subject Involvement. During the experiment, no human data was collected and no human participants were deceived or harmed. The only human data is WildChat, which is an open-source dataset of the dialogues between human users and LLM. (3) Data Safety. We release all the scripts and datasets we used in the Github repository for exhibition and reproduction. Since the defense method is adequate to intercept PAB, we are not concerned about the misuse of PAB with the deployment scripts. (4) Defense Method. We introduce Anti-PAB as a defense method against PAB, which is very light for every model to deploy. Whether the model is attacked or not, the developer can choose deploy this simple defense. The code of Anti-PAB is stored in the Github repository.

    Qwen 3.5 Models (Flash, Plus): Used as backbone models. Subject to the Tongyi Qianwen LICENSE AGREEMENT.

  • •

    Deepseek-V3.2: Used as the primary backbone and for metric evaluation. Released under the MIT License.

    GPT-5.1: Accessed via OpenAI API for ability bound tests. Used in accordance with OpenAI’s Terms of Use.
